TRANSCRIPT OF PROCEEDINGS
THE HON CATHERINE HOLMES AC SC, Commissioner
THE ROYAL COMMISSION INTO THE ROBODEBT SCHEME
DIRECTIONS HEARING
THURSDAY, 13 OCTOBER 2022 AT 10 AM (AEST)
DAY 2
MR JUSTIN GREGGERY KC, Senior Counsel Assisting
MR ANGUS SCOTT, Counsel Assisting
MS RENEE BERRY, Counsel Assisting
MS SALWA MARSH, Counsel Assisting
MS DOMINIQUE HOGAN-DORAN SC, for the Commonwealth

COMMISSIONER: I will take the appearances. Mr Greggery?
MR GREGGERY: Commissioner, I appear today with Mr Scott, Ms Berry and Ms Marsh.
COMMISSIONER: And Ms Hogan-Doran?
MS HOGAN-DORAN: Commissioner, I appear on behalf of the Commonwealth.
COMMISSIONER: Ms Hogan-Doran, the directions hearing is to do with responses to notices
to produce and notices to give. But there's another matter that I think might conveniently
be dealt with at the start, and that's the question of leave to appear for certain people and
the Commonwealth itself. It seems to me it would be simplest if I just advised you now that I
grant leave to appear to the Commonwealth throughout the Commission, and I grant leave
to appear to those persons who were ministers of the Department of Social Security and
Human Services - I think Social Services and Human Services, those people who were
secretaries of the department and I think there was the CEO of Services Australia, for the
period between the beginning of 2015 and the settlement of the class action, which was
November 2020.
That's purely on the basis that there's a level of responsibility there that would convince me
that they had an interest. It's not to say, of course, that anybody must appear or that we are
not looking at other people and other periods, but they are simply the ones that it seems to
me that it would be expeditious just to say that immediately, that they had that leave.
MS HOGAN-DORAN: Yes, Commissioner.
COMMISSIONER: Thank you. And now we turn to the subject matter of the directions
hearing. Mr Greggery?
MR GREGGERY: Yes. Thank you, Commissioner. The topic of the directions hearing today is
the delay on the part of the Commonwealth in producing information and documents in
accordance with the notices issued by the Commission. I will shortly tender a letter with five
annexures and attachments which identifies the matters outstanding as at 4 pm yesterday.
Before I tender those documents and address their content, I will provide some context.
And I note that the Commonwealth was informed of the - that copy of the letter and
attachments would be provided to you, Commissioner, in advance of the directions hearing
this morning, and I confirm that has occurred.
This Commission was announced by the Prime Minister on 25 August 2022, with a date to
report of 18 April 2023. The matters of the inquiry are set out in the Letters Patent, and they
make it plain that persons in position to provide evidence will largely be drawn from those
who were in the executive or legislative branches of government when the scheme was
established, implemented and ultimately discontinued. As I said at the initial hearing, much
has to be done to prepare for the first public hearing, and the appointment of the
Commission reflects contentions which have existed for a considerable period of time.

The materials sought by the notices will not be a surprise despite its volume, and the
turnaround time for production of material in response to the notices for the first hearing
will be short. Indeed, there is a degree of overlap between the issues identified in the
Letters Patent and the subject of enquiries in early 2017, although the terms of reference
are broader in some respects. But the troubled history of the scheme ought to have made it
more likely that documents prepared in response to questions raised about its various
stages are more easily produced.
The terms of the Letters Patent raised questions of legal professional privilege and public
interest immunity claims which had to be determined quickly. But, of course, all of that is
said with the acknowledgment that time is limited and the issues are complex. And the
Commonwealth requested notices to produce all documents in its possession, including
documents prepared and disclosed in the class action proceedings in the Federal Court. It, of
course, is entitled to adopt that position, but the obvious consequence is that in order to
fulfil its task that the Commissioner - or, rather, your task, the Commissioner should err on
the side of drafting notices more broadly rather than more narrowly because the
opportunity to consider readily available documents with a view to narrowing the scope of
the notices for the first hearing was lost.
However, I can indicate care was taken to ensure that notices were issued which would
minimise the burden on the recipient. The majority of notices to produce material from the
first hearing, which, of course, commences on 31 October, are directed to the government
departments responsible for the implementation of the scheme and particular persons
within those departments. All notices reflect the subjects of the Letters Patent, and
solicitors assisting the Commission adopted a process of sending draft notices to the
solicitors for the Commonwealth and inviting feedback in consultation with the proposed
recipient of those notices before they were issued in final form. That opportunity to
comment was not limited to feedback but included feedback about the scope of the notices
and the volume of material which might be produced in response.
On a number of occasions, feedback was not provided. On a number of occasions, a
complete response to the final notice was not produced by the due date, and that included
occasions where the inability to produce material on time was not foreshadowed. On a
number of occasions, requests for extension of time were sought by the Commonwealth,
and on most of those, and to the greatest extent possible, those extensions were granted by
the Commission.
I say that these are not matters of inconsequential procedural irregularity, although some of
them may be, for three reasons. First, section 3 of the Royal Commissions Act provides a
person who fails to produce a thing required by a notice commits an offence punishable by
imprisonment for up to two years. Notices should be understood in that light.
Secondly, delays in production of documents directly impairs the ability of those assisting
the Commission to prepare for the first hearing, for three reasons: the volume of the
material produced so far, more than 120,000 documents, with a further 100,000
foreshadowed late yesterday; the compressed timeframe of a little over two weeks for the

first hearing; and the need to consider the material before issuing notices to witnesses to
appear at the first hearing.
It is of some concern that the volume of material disclosed, and foreshadowed to be
disclosed, may reflect an inadequate screening process to ascertain what is truly responsive
to the notices. But, of course, those assisting the Commission are not in a position to say
one way or the other about that, apart from identifying duplications of documents and
some obviously irrelevant ones.
The third reason why this is not a matter of inconsequential procedural irregularity is the
flow-on effect. The second public hearing will commence on 5 December for a period of two
weeks. Notices to produce material for the second hearing are currently being drafted, and
some have been sent in draft form. The due date for those notices will not be later than the
last day of the first public hearing so that those assisting the Commission will be in a
position to use the three weeks available between the first and second hearing to fully
prepare.
Commissioner, I tender the letter from the solicitors assisting the Commission to the
solicitors for the Commonwealth dated 12 October 2022, with attachments. I understand
that exhibits tendered in the directions hearing today will be uploaded to the Commission's
website in due course.
COMMISSIONER: Yes, that will be marked as the first exhibit in the Commission's hearings.
The actual marking hasn't yet been decided, but it will be effectively exhibit number 1.
MR GREGGERY: Commissioner, because you have had a copy in advance, I don't propose to
go through the document in great detail. But I should note at the outset that - if I can take
the Commission to schedule A, which is the notice to give issued to the Commonwealth of
Australia, and page 3 of that notice. There is a reference to NTG0014, a notice to give a
statement and produce information issued to Services Australia. I inform the Commission
that a response has been provided to that notice since 4 pm yesterday, and its inclusion is
now a matter of history rather than present concern.
Otherwise, schedule A and B and the three letters, which are annexures to the letter, set out
what is currently outstanding, and those schedules generally speak for themselves. That
short table - or those two short tables are provided for clarification on the record about the
history of what was the position as at yesterday afternoon. And, accordingly, I seek the
assurance of the Commonwealth in three respects: firstly, that the material outstanding will
be provided forthwith; secondly, that the -
COMMISSIONER: Slow down a little, Mr Greggery.
MR GREGGERY: Sorry, Commissioner.
COMMISSIONER: Okay. Material outstanding to be provided forthwith.

MR GREGGERY: Secondly, that material sought in notices which are current - and a number
of those fall to be delivered towards the end of next week - will be produced on time; and
thirdly, that early indication be given by the Commonwealth of the specific circumstances in
where the time frames cannot be met. Of course, those assisting the Commission will
continue to accommodate requests which fall into that third category to the greatest extent
possible.
Before I complete what I have to say - I can indicate I have said what I need to in respect of
the main topic, but this is an opportunity to observe on an unrelated topic that the
Commission has received submissions through the website from a range of people who
were affected by the scheme in one way or another, or involved with it, and those who have
offered constructive insights into it. And those submissions are most welcomed and
welcomed on a continuing basis. Thank you, Commissioner.
COMMISSIONER: Thank you. Ms Hogan-Doran.
MS HOGAN-DORAN: Commissioner, I seek to address you with reference to two letters that
have been sent to the Commission, to those solicitors assisting. Could I just identify those
two letters which have been sent this morning.
COMMISSIONER: I think I have been provided with something. Thank you.
MS HOGAN-DORAN: Thank you, Commissioner. The first letter is a letter which is headed
Royal Commission into the Robodebt Scheme - Commonwealth Response, which I am
instructed was sent to the solicitors assisting at 10.22 am Canberra time, which would be
9.22 am Brisbane time. Commissioner, do you have that letter?
COMMISSIONER: Yes, I do.
MS HOGAN-DORAN: Thank you, Commissioner. I also propose to address you by reference
to a second letter which I'm instructed was sent to you at - sorry, I withdraw that - sent to
solicitors assisting at 9.55 am Brisbane time, which is 10.55 am Canberra time, which is
headed Royal Commission into the Robodebt Scheme - Commonwealth Response - Legal
Professional Privilege. Commissioner, do you have a copy of that second letter?
COMMISSIONER: And shall I mark them as exhibits?
MS HOGAN-DORAN: Yes, Commissioner.
COMMISSIONER: I direct they may be marked as exhibits. They can have separate exhibit
numbers. Yes. Thank you.
MS HOGAN-DORAN: Commissioner -
COMMISSIONER: They will effectively be 2 and 3, but what the ultimate number is - it may
be more complex than that.

MS HOGAN-DORAN: Thank you, Commissioner. I will refer to them in that way, if it is
convenient to you.
COMMISSIONER: Yes.
MS HOGAN-DORAN: Commissioner, might I just note - before I do that, I wish to note that
the assurances that have been sought by counsel assisting this morning, I will seek
instructions with respect to them. They were not the subject of earlier correspondence.
COMMISSIONER: All right. How long will that take you? Do you want a moment now or -
MS HOGAN-DORAN: Those assisting me will have heard what I've just said. I haven't had an
opportunity even to say to them: Please seek instructions.
COMMISSIONER: Okay.
MS HOGAN-DORAN: But perhaps if I could commence by addressing by reference to the
correspondence that has been sent, with a view to identifying a pragmatic and efficient
solution to the production - the outstanding production. Commissioner, the Commonwealth
is acutely aware that it is the central repository of evidence that is relevant to the work of
your Commission. The Commonwealth is working to respond to the notices the Commission
has issued in a timely way, and that is in as timely a way as the circumstances permit.
Those circumstances include but are not limited to the following matters. The first is
consideration by the Commonwealth of the complex issues that arise in relation to its
reliance on public interest immunity and legal professional privilege in the context of the
Commission's terms of reference. I will shortly take, Commissioner, to you in respect to
correspondence as to legal professional privilege and address you separately with respect to
the position on public interest immunity.
The second matter is the coordination of searches to be made by the Commonwealth across
its various agencies and departments for material that is responsive to the notices that have
been issued by the Commission to date, which I understand is something in the order of 23.
Thirdly, the coordination of the production of that material to the Commission in a manner
that will assist the Commission in its work, including both first and second review, or I think
as - counsel assisting referred or described it as a screening process.
And the fourth is the coordination of a consistent application across agencies, including the
departments, to the approach determined by the Commonwealth to be taken to public
interest immunity and legal professional privilege claims.
Commissioner, we would ask that you take into account that the Commonwealth is, of
course, experienced in dealing with the requirement to produce large volumes of material
to courts, tribunals, Royal Commissions and, of course, inquiries, and we ask that the
Commission - and submit that this Commission should evaluate the Commonwealth's

Commissioner, there has been an opportunity to comment on draft notices, and there has
been active work between those assisting you and those instructing me. And the
Commission, of course, knows the number of notices that it has issued, but we appreciate
that it does not yet have visibility of the scope of the material that is caught by the notices
as issued. In the time that the Commonwealth has had to establish for itself the scope and
nature of the exercise, it must undertake to comply with the Commission's notices. It has
become readily apparent that the scope of the notices is significantly broader than the
Commonwealth initially anticipated.
The letter, which I won't take your Honour - sorry, I withdraw that - Commissioner, I won't
take you through, but the letter then sets out, at the second page, instances or examples by
references to the notices to produce addressed to the agency Services Australia, and notices
addressed to the Department of Social Services, which are, respectively, recipients of
notices to both produce and to give a written statement.
One particular aspect of notices issued to both Services Australia and Social Services is
identification of documents and provision of a table as to an extremely broad category,
namely, all decisions made in respect of the Robodebt scheme as that is described in the
Letters Patent.
Commissioner, is it convenient that I then address the second letter, which, Commissioner,
you have marked - or indicated will be marked as exhibit 3. I appreciate that those
instructing you - those assisting you may not have had an opportunity to review this letter
given the time at which it was provided to the solicitors assisting.
COMMISSIONER: Can I just take up a couple of things with you first, Ms Hogan-Doran?
MS HOGAN-DORAN: Yes, Commissioner.
COMMISSIONER: As I recall, the election was in May this year. So from then, it was really
government policy that there would be a Commission of Inquiry into the Robodebt scheme.
So that can't have come as any surprise to Services Australia, and it also can't have come as
any surprise that, as a Commission of Inquiry into that scheme, the net would be flung wider
than it was in the Ombudsman's inquiries and the Senate's inquiries so that there was rather
a lot of time to be thinking about topics as broad as decisions made in respect of the
Robodebt scheme. It must have been fairly obvious that that kind of category of document
would be the subject of notices.
And having said that, and inviting your response, can I say I obviously take into account the
amount of work this is imposing on those instructing you, and I very much appreciate your
cooperation - their cooperation with the solicitors assisting the Commission. The problem is
we are all on a very tight line here, and it does seem that deadlines are not being met and
warnings not always been given that that would be the case. It seems that 10 o'clock
sometimes turns to 3 o'clock, and that really isn't satisfactory. So I don't know if you want to
deal with that now or if you would prefer to go on to the second letter.

MS HOGAN-DORAN: Commissioner, those that instruct me - and for my own observation, if
I may say - have been making genuine attempts to comply. There is, of course, a recognition
of the circumstances in which the Commission's Letters Patent were issued and the timeline
that the Commission has to - has set for itself to conduct public hearings and to prepare the
report. The scope of the notices has in - in giving effect to the searches, review and
production, has been compounded by the broadness and being - that it being broader than
was anticipated.
Now, one substantial aspect of production has been identifying the way in which the
Commonwealth would provide to the Commission documents which would be otherwise
the subject of legal professional privilege. The production of documents of that nature, it is
appreciated and understood, are raised squarely by at least two aspects of your terms of
reference, and there are earnest steps being taken to propose a way in which that material
can be provided expeditiously to the Commission and, indeed, key advices have been
provided already.
COMMISSIONER: Surely that's not a huge area of discovery, though, is it? I shouldn't have
thought there were hundreds of advices. I certainly hope not.
MS HOGAN-DORAN: The terms of the notices do not seek only production of the advices
but seek descriptions concerning the advices and, for example, actions taken in response to
a particular advice, communications concerning or relating to an advice. So it is the matrix of
what emerges from it.
COMMISSIONER: Yes. Even so, you would think that the focal advices must be limited in
number so that the number of documents surrounding in that respect can't be huge. But I
understand what you're saying.
MS HOGAN-DORAN: Yes. Commissioner, would it be of assistance if I identify the matters
set out in the second letter -
COMMISSIONER: Yes.
MS HOGAN-DORAN: - in that context? Thank you, Commissioner. Commissioner, the letter
is not before you, but it was communicated to -
COMMISSIONER: I'm sorry, which letter are we talking about? I've got one dated 13
October. Is that the -
MS HOGAN-DORAN: Yes, Commissioner. In paragraph 2 of that letter, reference is made to
a letter sent on 7 October 2022. That is the letter to which I am making reference.
COMMISSIONER: All right.
MS HOGAN-DORAN: But it is summarised adequately in that paragraph for current
purposes, that is, that on 7 October, the Australian Government Solicitor advised that the

documents and that it needed to give effect to that decision with respect to the production
of documents to the Commission and the provision of statements and information to the
Commission.
As I said earlier, Commissioner, the reason for that decision, that is, to advise you that the
Commonwealth intended to waive legal professional privilege in relation to certain
documents, was that the Commission, it is accepted, will need access to legal advice to be
able to fulfil its terms of reference, specifically the terms of reference which focus squarely
on legal advice and legal challenges in relation to the Robodebt scheme, in particular
paragraph (g) of your Letters Patent, being, "The establishment, design and implementation
of the Robodebt scheme, including," as is set out at (iv), "any concerns raised regarding the
legality or fairness of the Robodebt scheme"; and then terms of reference (i), being, "In
relation to concerns raised about the Robodebt scheme following its implementation," and
(v), "how the Australian Government responded to legal challenges or threatened legal
challenges."
Commissioner, this letter in paragraph 4, by way of assistance to you, Commissioner, as to
giving effect to the Commonwealth's decision to waive legal professional privilege with
respect to certain communications, the Commonwealth considers that the advices relating
to the legality of the Robodebt scheme created up to the date of 27 November 2019 are
likely to be the most directly relevant to the Letters Patent. That's because that is the date
the Federal Court of Australia declared, with the consent of the Australian Government, that
a demand for payment of an alleged debt under the Robodebt scheme was not validly
made. Accordingly, the Commonwealth will waive privilege in relation to those advices.
Just pausing there, Commissioner, if I may, I think it's set out in the schedules that counsel
assisting has provided - and as now set out again in paragraph 5 of this letter, the
Commonwealth has already provided a collection of legal advices of this kind, including the
advice of the Solicitor-General, in the hope that that will assist the Commissioners - the
Commission, and those assisting you, their preparation for the 31 October '22 hearing.
Those were 10 legal advices that relate to the notice to give a statement of information,
number 1, issued to Services Australia on 11 October, and 17 legal advices that relate to the
notice to give a statement of information, number 2, issued to the Department of Social
Services. And those 17 legal advices were provided on 7 October. Commissioner, I confirm
that the Commonwealth waives legal professional privilege in relation to those advices and
understands that the Commission will tender, use and disclose those advices as it sees fit.
Commissioner, you have already identified that there are a key number of legal advices and
a quantum of legal advices that can be identified by number. But as I have indicated to you,
there are a range of ways in which those advices have been sought by those assisting you to
be addressed in the production of documents and in the statements of information.
What the balance of the letter from paragraph 8 sets out is how the Commonwealth
proposes that other legal advices that the Commonwealth would likely waive legal
professional privilege over but which have not yet been produced to the Commission will be

managed, and that is with respect to what is, with respect, a large volume of material that is
involved.
The issue that is addressed in paragraph 9 is an appreciation that there may be
communications which - of a legally privileged nature which may go - which may not be
directly relevant to the terms of reference in the Letters Patent.
COMMISSIONER: And, sorry -
MS HOGAN-DORAN: And the Commonwealth -
COMMISSIONER: Sorry, Ms Hogan-Doran. I just want to make sure we are looking at the
same thing. Did you just say paragraph 9 dealt with this issue?
MS HOGAN-DORAN: Yes.
COMMISSIONER: My paragraph 9 is, "The Commonwealth is conscious of the need for a
pragmatic and efficient solution." This is the 13 October letter. Am I looking at the right
thing?
MS HOGAN-DORAN: Commissioner, may I just pause for a moment. It would appear that
the document - could I just seek some further instructions in relation to the document that
you hold and the document that I hold.
COMMISSIONER: All right. You may have an older version or I may. We will find out, I guess.
MS HOGAN-DORAN: Thank you, Commissioner. Just one moment, if I may. Commissioner,
could I just indicate that a copy of the document that you have is being sought and will be
provided to me shortly. The document I have is not the document that you have.
COMMISSIONER: No. Well, that seems evident. Mine has, all together, 12 paragraphs. So I
don't know if I'm missing something critical. But, Ms Hogan-Doran, I see that what you are
proposing is a way of producing the balance of legal records but maintaining privilege,
handing them over but saying, "We are not giving away privilege. You have to tell us before
you want to use it." That's something I thought you might have sorted out with the
solicitors assisting the Commission and counsel. It doesn't really address the problems we
are about to hear today, does it, which is that delivery so far has been late, not when
indicated, not always with an explanation of delay. I mean, this - this sort of thing may well
be able to be sorted out. I don't know that we were really meaning to have a directions
hearing about this, though.
How are you getting on with the instructions for the three things Mr Greggery asked for? I
think what we really want to do today is make it clear that we need things when they are
asked for or on an extension where that's explained and granted, that they have to turn up
at the time appointed, that it's no good just letting things drag so it's the next day or much
later the same day. And what is really wanted from the Commonwealth is an assurance that

of provision won't continue. And I'm sure it's the cry of every Royal Commission,
Ms Hogan-Doran. I'm sure these problems arise every time.
MS HOGAN-DORAN: Yes. I accept that, Commissioner, and I have experience of other Royal
Commissions. And those that are instructing me and those who are working across the
Commonwealth are conscious of the needs of this Commission and are making genuine
attempts, and substantial resources have been deployed, and are being deployed, given that
the Commission is - the Commonwealth is the central repository of the material that will be
necessary for your work.
COMMISSIONER: Well, are you in a position yet to assure me that the outstanding material
will be provided straightaway, as in, 5 pm today?
MS HOGAN-DORAN: No, Commissioner.
COMMISSIONER: And presumably the other two matters, which are that the current notices
will be late and that there be an early indication of why and how it is that a time can't be
met so something else can be arranged if it is essential.
MS HOGAN-DORAN: Commissioner, I will just have those instructions confirmed. The - in
paragraph 1, the first assurance that was sought was that material would be provided
forthwith. The communications that have previously been made to the Commission would
be that material other than which is the subject of legal professional privilege and public
interest immunity were foreshadowed to be provided by the end of this week, which is
tomorrow, as opposed to today. The - and what has been - what is said with respect to the
practical approach, which I accept is something that could be communicated further
between those instructing me and those assisting you but has been brought - because of the
directions hearing, brought directly to the directions hearing for -
COMMISSIONER: All right.
MS HOGAN-DORAN: - consideration would mean if that position is accepted with respect to
legal professional privilege, the instructions that I have is that that material will be able to
be transferred from the Commission's providers within a matter of hours.
The - as to communications concerning current notices and those that will be due at the end
of next week, the Commonwealth has heard what has been said as to the utility of there
being greater communication between the Commission and - sorry, between the
Commonwealth and the Commission so that if deadlines are unable to be met, there are
specific circumstances identified as to why that is and proposals made so that an
appropriate extension of time can be given.
The third assurance that was sought was that an early indication be given as to those
specific circumstances. That has been the endeavour - on my own observation, that has
been the endeavour to date, and there's no reason why that wouldn't be the position going
forward.

COMMISSIONER: All right. Ms Hogan-Doran, would it be helpful if we went back to
Mr Greggery now so that he can respond to that and also to the proposal that the legal
professional privilege material be handed over with the caveat that you have identified so I
can hear what he has to say about it? Are you happy if that happens?
MS HOGAN-DORAN: If that's convenient to you, Commissioner.
COMMISSIONER: All right. Thank you. Mr Greggery, do you want to respond?
MR GREGGERY: Yes. I can confirm to my learned friend the proposal in paragraph 10 of the
letter that I have is acceptable to the solicitors assisting the Commission. The second point is
in respect of the assurance that outstanding matters are hoped or intended or
foreshadowed to be provided by the end of this week - those assurances in similarly broad
terms have been made previously and not always delivered upon. And we are now not
much more than two weeks away from the start of the Commission. So something more
concrete is sought from the Commission.
There remains the outstanding question of the determination of public interest immunity,
and it was under consideration a week ago. At least, it was communicated to us that it was
under consideration a week ago. We are not sure when a decision will be made on that and
whether any information can be provided about it. And a note of not particularly great
significance is that the second exhibit, the letter of 12 October 2022, the Commission was
taken to paragraph 9 which described a request for decisions made in respect of the
Robodebt scheme was extremely broad. The notice NTG0001, of course, limited decisions to
those made by ministers and members of the senior executive service, so not as broad as it
might have been conveyed. But those are the matters that I can respond to immediately.
COMMISSIONER: All right. Coming back to you, Ms Hogan-Doran, do we have an assurance
at the outset that material will be provided by close of business tomorrow? And do we have
an assurance - sorry, did you get that? Do we have an assurance that the outstanding
material will be provided by close of business tomorrow? Close of business in most normal
circumstances meaning 5 pm, but you get an hour's daylight-saving grace here.
MS HOGAN-DORAN: Commissioner, with respect to the legal professional privilege
material, which is a substantial amount of material, on the basis that is set out in the
correspondence, that can be done. I give you the assurance that that will be provided on
that basis. The - with respect to public interest immunity claims, the documents that are the
subject of such claims, Mr Greggery is correct in saying that it was under consideration. It is
under consideration at the highest level - urgent consideration at the highest level, but I'm
not in a position yet to be able to communicate an assurance as to production with respect
to that issue. With respect to the other documents - in respect of the other categories, I can
only give you assurance as to some but not all for production by tomorrow afternoon at 5
pm Brisbane time.
COMMISSIONER: Why is that?

MS HOGAN-DORAN: There's a number of reasons. Those include - in part, just the simple
mechanics of completing the reviews and the volume of the documentation that has - is the
subject of those reviews.
COMMISSIONER: All right. Look, I don't know that we can do much better than say that
those instructing you should certainly aim to have that material produced by 5 pm and to
have communication with the solicitors for the Commission much earlier if, in fact, there is
going to be any delay. And I wouldn't imagine that much more delay can be afforded on this
material at all. And so if we are talking delay, maybe by tomorrow - by Saturday morning at
the worst. But it has to happen. These - you know, sliding deadlines just can't continue. In
relation to the legal professional privilege material, you had spoken to it being available
within hours. That doesn't have to wait until 5 pm tomorrow, presumably?
MS HOGAN-DORAN: Commissioner, the provision is - the materials are with our document
management provider. So provided - following a quality check, that material would be able
to be transferred to the Commission's provider within a matter of hours. That is what I have
been instructed. There will be a number of steps just before that, that is, identifying what
that material is. It will be, in a global sense, communicating to the provider and that being
giving effect to. So it may not be by 5 pm today, but it's certainly within the scope of the
assurance you sought for tomorrow afternoon.
COMMISSIONER: Yes. I was thinking about other documents when I asked for that
assurance. It doesn't seem that we've got an awful lot further here. Mr Greggery, do you
have any suggestions?
MR GREGGERY: No, I appreciate - other than to observe that Ms Hogan-Doran is, of course,
limited by her instructions. But to the extent that they've been solicited in this hearing, they
are consistent with the sliding nature of communications and in respect of deadlines so far.
The reference to a number of hours appears at paragraph 12 of exhibit 3 in my copy, which
didn't appear to have the caveats on the timeframe that were just identified by my learned
friend.
MS HOGAN-DORAN: Commissioner, could I indicate I have the same letter as you now.
